food.text: After the Arab conquest of Egypt in 641 CE, Egyptian cooks began working with newly introduced crops such as rice, sugarcane, and citrus fruits, grown in the fertile land watered by the Nile. Egypt's position at the heart of the Islamic world also drew Turks, Kurds, and Persians whose cooking traditions blended with and enriched local Egyptian food.

In the villages around Aswan, Nubian cooking was built around locally grown barley, sorghum, and wheat from the Nile Valley. A traditional bread called kabed, made by mixing corn flour with water into a dough baked crisp at the edges but soft inside, was commonly eaten with milk, honey, vegetables, or meat.

Nilometers recorded the Nile's flood level each year. A moderate flood was vital to the agricultural cycle. A lighter flood than normal would cause famine, and too much water was equally disastrous, washing away much of the infrastructure built on the floodplain. Priests monitored the day-to-day level of the river to predict the coming flood, and the quality of the flood was used to set tax levels.

Beginning in 962, a series of unusually low Nile floods struck Egypt, and hot winds and locust swarms further destroyed crops, bringing on the worst famine in living memory. A rat-borne plague added to the crisis, striking a population already weakened by severe food shortages.

One of the nilometers that still survives today stands on the island of Roda in Cairo, built in AD 861 on the order of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil and overseen by the astronomer al-Farghani. Its readings tracked the Nile's rise so officials could judge whether that year's flood would bring a good harvest or a shortfall.

By 968, Egypt's famine had driven food prices to extraordinary heights: a chicken cost 25 times its pre-famine price, and an egg fifty times as much. Fustat, then the most populous city in the Islamic world after Baghdad, suffered most heavily, with disease outbreaks continuing into the early years of Fatimid rule.

Records from AD 622 to 999 show that, on average, 28% of the years brought a Nile flood that fell short of expectations. Since a lighter inundation than normal would cause famine, communities that depended entirely on the river's yearly rise faced hunger in more than one year in four.

According to the Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi (d. 1442), mulukhiyah was the favorite dish of Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, founder of the Umayyad Caliphate, who ruled from 661 to 680. The dish was already known in the medieval Arab world.

Nilometers used across Egypt came in three basic designs: a vertical column marked off in cubits, a stairway of steps leading down to the river's edge, or a deep well linked to the Nile by a culvert. These different designs let officials in various locations still track the flood consistently enough to judge the year's expected harvest.

art.text: In Nubia, the Christian kingdom of Makuria reached a cultural peak that began in the 9th century. It built the Throne Hall of Dongola, the great cruciform church of Dongola and the Banganarti monastery. Its artists also developed wall paintings and finely crafted, decorated pottery.

After the Muslim conquest of Egypt in the 7th century, Islamic architecture flourished. A new capital, Fustat, was founded and became the center of monumental architectural patronage. Through successive new administrative capitals, it eventually became the modern city of Cairo.

Little Egyptian music was notated before the 7th century, when Egypt became part of the Muslim world. At that time percussion and vocal music became important in Egyptian music. They have remained important ever since.

Early Islamic architecture in Egypt mixed several influences. These included classical antiquity and new ones from the east, such as the Abbasid style. That style radiated in the 9th century from the Abbasid Caliphate's heartland in Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq.

Dongola, the capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, was founded around 500 in the fertile Dongola Reach. Soon after, in the mid-6th century, Makuria converted to Christianity. The city later held the Throne Hall and the great cruciform church.

Archaeological evidence shows increased Makurian influence on the art and architecture of Alodia from the 8th century. Alodia was the southern Nubian kingdom that shared a border with Makuria. This suggests that artistic styles spread between the two Nubian realms.
In the 10th century, Egypt became the center of a new empire, the Fatimid Caliphate. Fatimid architecture initiated further developments that influenced the architectural styles of later periods.

There is little notation of Egyptian music before the 7th century AD, when Egypt became part of the Muslim world. At that time percussion and vocal music became important. They have remained an important part of Egyptian music ever since.

At the end of the 7th century, the Church of the Granite Columns was built at Old Dongola over an earlier church, adorned with 16 granite columns topped with richly decorated capitals. It is thought to have served as the cathedral of Old Dongola.

war.text: In 651/652 a Rashidun Arab army led by Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi al-Sarh invaded Makuria and besieged and bombarded Dongola with catapults. They damaged parts of the town but could not penetrate the walls of the citadel, and Muslim sources highlight the skill of the Nubian archers in repelling them. With neither side able to win, Abi Sarh and King Qalidurut agreed the Baqt treaty, which ensured largely uninterrupted peace between Egypt and Makuria until the 13th century. It began as a ceasefire with an annual exchange of Makurian slaves for Egyptian wheat, textiles and other goods.

In 651 Abdallah ibn Sa'd marched 5,000 men to Dongola, equipped with heavy cavalry and a catapult. He then besieged the city, which put his cavalry in the precarious position of storming a walled city defended by the infamous Nubian archers.

In 642 a Muslim expedition reached Dongola and met strong Makurian resistance, especially from Nubian archers, whose arrows came down in showers. Many Muslims returned wounded, including with eye injuries, and the Nubians were called "pupil smiters" for their skill at hitting opponents' eyes. Al-Baladhuri quotes a man who visited Nubia twice under Umar: the Nubians formed a line, the Muslims wanted to use swords but could not, and the Nubians "put out eyes to the number of one hundred and fifty." The expedition then withdrew from Nubia.

Amr ibn al-As ended the first Dongola campaign because of the difficulty of the campaign, the limited prospect of booty, and the effectiveness of the Nubian military. Arab accounts say the Nubians shot from a distance and avoided close combat, so the Muslims could not use their swords while Nubian arrows wounded many of them and put out the eyes of 150. The expedition was frustrated rather than defeated in one big battle.

In mid-658 Mu'awiya sent a Syrian army of approximately 6,000 troops under Amr ibn al-As to annex Egypt, and Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr could muster only 2,500 loyalist troops. At the Battle of al-Musanna the larger Syrian and Uthmanid force swiftly overwhelmed the Egyptians; the Alid commander Kinana ibn Bishr was killed in the heat of battle and Muhammad's lines collapsed. Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr tried to flee but was captured and executed by the forces of Mu'awiya ibn Hudayj, and Egypt was incorporated into the Umayyad domain, depriving the Alid caliphate of vital tax revenues and isolating its power base in Iraq.

John the Deacon claims that before 747 the Umayyad governor of Egypt imprisoned the Coptic Patriarch, prompting a Makurian invasion and siege of Fustat, after which the Patriarch was released. The episode has been called Christian Egyptian propaganda, but Upper Egypt was likely subject to a Makurian campaign, perhaps a raid.

Archaeology shows Dongola was well fortified in the seventh century. Its mudbrick walls, faced with stone, were at least 6 metres high and 4 metres wide at the base. Round corner towers projected 8 metres from the wall, and they may have been added in response to the siege of 652.

According to al-Maqrizi, the Makurians had never seen the catapult (manjaniq) that Abdallah brought to Dongola, probably a traction trebuchet. During the siege its fire damaged the town's cathedral, and a damaged mid-seventh-century church has been found outside the city walls.

In 657 Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, Ali's new governor, abandoned neutrality and told the rebels to pledge allegiance or leave Egypt. This triggered a revolt under Mu'awiya ibn Hudayj. Muhammad's first offensive under Al-Harith ibn Jumhan al-Ju'fi failed when Al-Harith was killed in the fighting, and a second expedition under Ibn Mudahim al-Kalbi also failed. Ali then sent Malik al-Ashtar to take command, but he was poisoned at Qulzum, an act widely attributed to Mu'awiya's instigation, and his death was celebrated in Damascus.

Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam wrote that Abdallah ended the siege because he was unable to defeat the Makurians. The Shiite historian Ahmad al-Kufi said Muslims had never suffered a loss like the one in Nubia. Later Muslim historians nonetheless recast the siege as a victory.

literature.text: The Coptic Alexander Romance, translated from Greek, attained its definitive form in the 6th century. What survives is a fragmentary text from the White Monastery, covering Alexander the Great among the Elamites, his rescue from the abyss in Gedrosia, his meeting with the Brahmans and his poisoning. The romance was clearly intended for monks' reading.

Old Nubian, one of the oldest written African languages, is attested in writing from the 8th to the 15th century CE. It survives in more than a hundred pages of religious and administrative texts, including homilies, prayers, psalms and legal documents and letters, written in an alphabet adapted from Coptic and used across the kingdom of Makuria.

Sahidic Coptic flourished as Egypt's leading literary language from about 325 to 800 CE, spoken in the region between Asyut and Oxyrhynchus. It was eventually overtaken by the Bohairic dialect of Lower Egypt, which gained prominence in the 9th century.

Bohairic Coptic, the dialect of Egypt's western Nile Delta, has its earliest attestation in the 4th century CE, though most texts date from the 9th century onward. By the 11th century it had overtaken Sahidic, which had earlier been the dominant written form of Coptic.

The original manuscript of the Coptic Alexander Romance had 220 pages divided into 37 chapters, each opening with a verse from the Bible. It portrayed Alexander the Great as a prophet who foreshadowed Christ, intended as reading material for monks.

The Old Nubian script, a slanted uncial version of the Coptic alphabet from the White Monastery, added extra letters partly borrowed from the Meroitic alphabet. It seems to have already existed by the 6th century, after the Meroitic state's collapse, though its earliest surviving texts date only to the 8th century.

Monastic sites in Egypt were also places of writing and memory. Coptic literary production, libraries, sermons, biblical copying and letters linked monastic communities to the spread of Coptic and to the preservation of Egyptian Christian traditions. Monks were major agents in creating the textual culture of late antique Egypt.

In the latter half of the 7th century, prominent Coptic writers included the Patriarchs Benjamin I and Agathon, along with Samuel of Qalamun, Isaac of Qalamun, John of Nikiu and Menas of Nikiu. Coptic literary production continued actively despite the recent Arab conquest of Egypt.

Bishop John of Nikiu, relying on eyewitness testimony, wrote a Chronicle giving a graphic account of the Muslim invasion of Egypt in 639 from a Coptic perspective. He says the invaders "despoiled the Egyptians of their possessions and dealt cruelly with them", and that after pulling down the city walls they "put to the sword thousands of its inhabitants and of the soldiers", took the women and children captive and divided them among themselves, and made the city a desolation. He also says the commander Amr ibn al-As "had no mercy on the Egyptians", though he adds that Amr later took none of the Churches' property. The Chronicle survives only in an Ethiopic translation, but some scholars believe it was first written in Coptic.

From the 10th century, Old Nubian became the main language of civil and religious administration in the kingdom of Makuria. It was used alongside Koine Greek, which remained widespread especially in religious contexts, and Coptic, which mainly predominated in funerary inscriptions.
After the Muslim conquest, papyrus was replaced by cloth paper as the writing material in Egypt. Calligraphy was also introduced as a writing system, changing how Egyptian writers worked.

According to the 10th-century diplomat al-Aswani, people of the southern Nubian kingdom of Alwa owned Greek books which they translated into their own language. About twenty inscriptions found at Musawwarat es-Sufra, Meroe and Soba suggest they used a distinct script, tentatively called Alwa Nubian.

Bishop Severus ibn al-Muqaffa, who died in 987, complained that Egypt's Coptic Christians no longer knew the Coptic language. He responded by composing a theological text in Arabic, becoming the first Coptic author to write such a work in that language.

science.text: In the 10th century, the geographer Al-Muqaddasi described the tall residential buildings of Fustat, Egypt's first capital under Muslim rule, as reaching seven storeys and looking like minarets. These high-rises could reportedly house hundreds of people.

In early medieval Egypt, farmers of every faith tracked the year's three farming seasons, each four months long, using the Coptic calendar. The calendar divided the year into twelve 30-day months, plus a short intercalary month of five or six days to keep it accurate.

Ahmad ibn Tulun's mosque in Cairo, built between 876 and 879 CE, was inspired by the 9th-century mosques of Samarra in Iraq, then the Abbasid capital. Its minaret has an unusual form, with an external spiral staircase winding around the outside.

Nubian churches built during this era featured vaults made entirely of mudbrick. The technique used only pure earth and required no timber at all, allowing long-lasting vaulted roofs to be built across the region.

At Old Dongola, capital of Makuria, a massive defence-like building known as the Throne Hall was built in the 9th century on a rocky spur beside the old fortress. Rising two storeys, it is thought to have been the ceremonial hall where the Makurian kings held court.

Around 856, al-Farghani wrote a treatise on the astrolabe in Cairo. He also supervised the building of the large New Nilometer on Rawda Island, completed in 861, an instrument that let people measure the height of the Nile in a flood.
The Throne Hall at Old Dongola measured 28 by 18 by 12 metres, with two storeys. Its ground-floor walls stood 6.5 metres high, while the upper floor's walls were 3.5 metres tall.
The Coptic calendar follows a leap year every four years without exception, like the Julian calendar. The Gregorian calendar, unlike the Coptic, skips three leap years every 400 years.

According to the 10th-century author Balawi, the architect of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun was a man named al-Nasrani, a non-Muslim who was possibly Christian. He had previously designed the Aqueduct of Basatin, another of Ibn Tulun's construction projects in the area.

politics.text: In AD 642, the Arab conquest of Egypt brought an end to the region's millennium-long Greco-Roman period. Before that, Egypt had been invaded or conquered by many foreign civilizations, including the Hyksos, the Kushites, the Assyrians, the Persians, the Greeks and the Romans.

From the time Roman forces conquered it in 30 BC until AD 642, most of modern-day Egypt was ruled as the imperial province of Aegyptus. The Roman Empire was later divided in two, and Egypt found itself in the Eastern Empire, whose capital was Constantinople. The last few centuries of this period have been called late antique Egypt.

Justinian I and his wife, the augusta Theodora, both sought to convert the Noba to Christianity. Justinian's envoys promoted dyophysitism, but the Noba were persuaded to adopt the miaphysitism of the Coptic Church by emissaries of the empress.

Makuria's rulers and the Muslim rulers of Egypt agreed to a treaty called the Baqt after several failed invasions. Nubians made an annual payment of slaves and other tribute to the Islamic Governor at Aswan, and runaway slaves were returned to Nubia. The treaty was kept for six hundred years.

Greek remained the language of government and trade in Egypt until the Muslim conquest of 641 AD. Alexandria kept its status as one of the leading cities of the Mediterranean well into the late Middle Ages.

Helped by the newly converted Noba, the Roman army conquered the pagan Blemmyes. In 543 the general Narses was sent to confiscate the cult statues of Philae, which were sent to Constantinople, to close the temple, and to suppress its priesthood by imprisonment.
The Arab conquest of 639-646 altered Egypt's political and cultural setting. Yet material and documentary evidence suggests substantial continuities in the first generations of Islamic rule.
Justin I ruled the Roman Empire from 518 to 527. In the early 6th century, during his reign, the Blemmyes again made attacks on Upper Egypt.

Mamluks were manumitted slaves who, after training in martial arts, court etiquette and Islamic sciences, were freed but expected to remain loyal to their master. They formed part of the military apparatus in Syria and Egypt since at least the 9th century, rising to become the Tulunid and Ikhshidid governing dynasties.

In 577, during Justin II's retirement and the start of Tiberius II Constantine's reign, the defences at Philae had to be rebuilt. They were needed to repel attacks by the Blemmyes, who were still threatening the frontier decades after Narses closed the temple.

Ali sent Malik al-Ashtar from Nisibis to take supreme command of Egypt, but he was poisoned at Qulzum. The act was widely attributed to the instigation of Mu'awiya, and Al-Ashtar's death was celebrated in Damascus. It left Muhammad isolated at his post.
In 750, after the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate, the sons of Marwan II, the last Umayyad Caliph, fled to Nubia. They asked King Kyriakos of Makuria for asylum, but without success.

philosophy.text: Most Egyptian Christians rejected the doctrine of two natures in Christ set out at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 CE. They held instead to miaphysitism, the doctrine of one united divine nature. By the sixth century the Coptic Church had its own independent hierarchy, led by the Pope of Alexandria and a governing synod.

Islam was introduced to Egypt in the seventh century CE during the early Muslim conquests. It began a profound religious transformation that would eventually make Egypt a major center of the Islamic world.

Between the fifth and twelfth centuries, the Christian kingdoms of Nubia controlled what is now Sudan. They delayed the expansion of Islam through a peace and trade treaty, known as the Baqt, with the ruling Muslim power in Cairo.

The Egyptian holy man became a major figure in late antique religion. Ascetics, monks, bishops and saints were represented as healers, exorcists, judges, prophets and mediators of divine power. Frankfurter argues that holy men could oppose older cults while also reorganizing older expectations about demons, spirits and blessing.

Al-Azhar was founded in 970 CE by the Fatimids as the first Islamic university in Egypt. It is one of two major religious institutions in Egypt, the other being the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria, established in the middle of the 1st century by Saint Mark.

Even when new religions supplanted older ones in Egypt, Egyptians frequently reinterpreted them through inherited cultural lenses. Customs such as funerary laments and ideas about the afterlife can be traced to ancient Egyptian origins, having survived inside later religious identities.

culture.text: Scribes no longer studied to read and write Egyptian hieroglyphs, and from roughly the 5th century CE the script became totally inscrutable. It stayed that way until its decipherment in the early 19th century. In the meantime, Egypt's own recorded history was rendered inaccessible.
culture.source_title: Ancient Egypt in the Western imagination

culture.text: Late antique Egypt did not end at a single moment. The Arab conquest altered political authority, but many older practices continued into the early Islamic period. Greek and Coptic documents, Christian communities, monasteries, textile production, burial practices, and forms of dress and adornment all show continuity as well as change.

Arabic came to Egypt in the 7th century. Today it is the formal and official language of the state, used by the government and newspapers. The Egyptian Arabic dialect, Masri, is the spoken language of the people.

Egypt was an early centre of Christianity, and the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria was founded in the first century. With the arrival of Islam in the seventh century, Egypt was gradually Islamised. It is unknown when Muslims became a majority, with estimates ranging from c. 1000 CE to as late as the 14th century.

Coptic did not simply replace Greek in late antique Egypt. Greek remained central to administration, education, and elite culture. Coptic became increasingly significant for biblical translation, monastic literature, letters, sermons, and eventually documents of daily life, and Choat argues it developed where Greek and Egyptian worlds met.

Everyday objects from late antique Egypt show how Christian identity was worn and carried. Cross pendants, inscribed bracelets, and amuletic bells served as protective objects. They often continued older habits of using objects to mediate power.

Dress objects, beads, bracelets, shoes, sandals, spindle whorls, toys, bells, and domestic tools survive from late antique Egypt. Together they show how people performed social roles and experienced daily life. Textile production and forms of dress and adornment kept going into the early Islamic period.

Coptic is the most recent stage of the Egyptian language. It is written mainly in the Greek alphabet with seven demotic letters added. Today it is the liturgical language of the Coptic Orthodox Church.
